What is the essential teaching in 'Discourses of the Ancient Nuns: (Bhikkhuni-samyutta)'?

In 'Discourses of the Ancient Nuns: (Bhikkhuni-samyutta)', the teaching opens with this observation: *"The growing interest in women's spirituality has led to a renewed focus upon the Therigatha, the Verses of the Elder Nuns, as the oldest existing testament to the feminine experience of Buddhism."* The central invitation is to turn one's investigation inward — to verify the Dhamma not as a set of beliefs, but as directly observable reality in one's own body, speech, and mind. As the text teaches, the Dhamma is *akāliko* — ever-present — and *opanayiko* — leading inward — available to be known (*paccattaṁ*) by each practitioner for themselves. There is no need to search elsewhere; the truth is already here.

Can you explain the teaching in the section '(Samyutta Nikaya, Book V)'?

This section teaches: *"[128] Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Savatthi in Jeta's Grove, Anathapindika's Park.
Then, in the morning, the bhikkhuni Alavika dressed and, taking bowl and robe, entered Savatthi for alms. [1] When she had walked for alms in Savatthi and had returned from her alms round, after her meal she went to the Blind Men..."* The core instruction is to turn investigation inward (*opanayiko*) toward what is already present in body, speech, and mind — not to seek the Dhamma outside or in future states. Whatever theme this section addresses, the method is the same: sustained, patient, non-grasping awareness that allows the truth to reveal itself. As Ajahn Mun taught: when the mind sees clearly, there is no longer any need to go looking.

This text mentions suffering (dukkha). Can you explain its role in practice?

In this text, dukkha appears in this context: *"Emerging from the depths of indubitable personal realization, crackling with insight, they point unwaveringly toward the rugged path of renunciation and wisdom that leads to the end of suffering."* Understanding suffering (dukkha) is not merely conceptual — it is meant to be verified directly. The Dhamma is *ehipassiko*: 'come and see for yourself.' Bring the quality described by dukkha into direct investigation: where is it present in your current experience? When seen clearly, each of these Pāli terms dissolves from abstract concept into living reality.

Why does the preceptor teach the five meditation themes at ordination?

The text explains: *"When she heard that Khema had gone forth under the Buddha, she visited her and was so inspired by their conversation that she too decided to take ordination."* The five themes — hair of head (kesā), hair of body (lomā), nails (nakhā), teeth (dantā), skin (taco) — are not arbitrary. They target the root of infatuation with the body. The skin, as the outermost layer, is what we are actually attracted to when we conceive of a body as beautiful. Contemplating the skin as a wrapping that holds together otherwise repulsive components directly undercuts sensual desire. This is the very first teaching given to a new monk — showing that the entire path begins with honest, unflinching investigation of the body.
